title: Myasthenic Crisis
bottomLine: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory or bulbar failure from severe neuromuscular weakness. Normal SpO2 can coexist with failing ventilation, so cough, secretion handling, voice, swallowing, work of breathing, CO2 signs, and ordered respiratory-force trends matter.
recognize: Fatigable weakness with weak cough or voice
Shallow breathing or rapidly increasing fatigue
differentiate: GBS is typically ascending areflexic neuropathy
Cholinergic excess adds prominent muscarinic symptoms
assessment: Airway, ventilation, cough and secretion clearance
management: Give crisis-directed IVIG/plasma exchange as ordered
Treat the trigger and conserve energy
medicationSafety: Airway safety outranks routine pyridostigmine timing
Review drugs that may worsen neuromuscular transmission
counselling: Report infection and medication changes early
examTrap: Waiting for oxygen desaturation before recognizing ventilatory failure.
oneLinePearl: Myasthenic crisis: watch ventilation and bulbar strength, not SpO2 alone.

title: Guillain-Barré Syndrome
bottomLine: GBS causes rapidly progressive peripheral nerve weakness, often ascending, with areflexia and possible respiratory, bulbar, or autonomic failure. Trend strength and ventilation before obvious distress appears.
differentiate: Stroke is focal and central rather than symmetric ascending areflexia
Myasthenia is fatigable junction weakness without the classic ascending sensory pattern
management: IVIG or plasma exchange as prescribed
medicationSafety: Corticosteroids are not standard disease-modifying therapy for GBS
IVIG has infusion, thrombosis, and renal risks
counselling: Report breathing or swallowing change immediately
examTrap: Focusing on leg weakness while missing respiratory or autonomic decline.
oneLinePearl: GBS ascends—monitor lungs and autonomics before weakness reaches them.

title: Meningococcal Meningitis and Sepsis
bottomLine: Invasive meningococcal disease can become shock or meningitis within hours. Start droplet precautions and emergency assessment on suspicion; tests must not create avoidable antimicrobial delay in a critically ill client.
recognize: Shock may occur without an early rash
differentiate: Viral meningitis cannot be safely assumed at triage
Purpura with shock is not a benign viral rash
medicationSafety: Do not delay empiric therapy for every test
Contact prophylaxis is separately directed by public health or medical order
examTrap: Waiting for the classic rash or LP before acting.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada invasive meningococcal guidance

title: Convulsive Status Epilepticus
bottomLine: A prolonged or recurrent convulsive seizure without recovery is time-critical. Protect airway and safety, time the seizure, check glucose early, give ordered benzodiazepine rescue promptly, and monitor ventilation after treatment.
recognize: Persistent coma after convulsions may represent ongoing seizure
differentiate: Syncope is brief with rapid recovery
Psychogenic events should not be assumed before dangerous causes are excluded
workup: EEG, imaging, or LP as indicated
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines can depress respiration and BP
No objects in mouth or oral medication during seizure
counselling: Medication adherence and seizure plan after stabilization
examTrap: Restraining the client or delaying rescue medication for nonessential testing.
oneLinePearl: Status: time it, glucose it, treat it, support breathing.
sourceBasis: Canadian emergency and neurology seizure practice

title: Cauda Equina Syndrome
bottomLine: New urinary retention or overflow, saddle anesthesia, bilateral sciatica, or progressive leg weakness with back pain is cauda equina syndrome until urgently assessed. Delayed decompression can make bladder, bowel, sexual, and motor deficits permanent.
recognize: Progressive leg weakness or new bowel/sexual dysfunction
differentiate: Routine sciatica lacks saddle anesthesia and sphincter dysfunction
Conus or spinal-cord lesions have overlapping red flags and are also urgent
assessment: Perineal sensory and lower-limb neuro assessment
medicationSafety: Analgesia must not delay neurologic reassessment
Do not label retention an opioid effect without checking neurologic red flags
counselling: Explain surgical urgency without promising recovery
followUp: Bladder, bowel, mobility, and rehabilitation follow-up
examTrap: Treating new urinary retention as simple UTI or medication effect in a back-pain client.
oneLinePearl: Back pain + saddle numbness + bladder change = emergency spine assessment.
